rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Kinematics begins with three vectors: **position** (location from an origin), **velocity** (rate of change of position, $v = dr/dt$) and **acceleration** (rate of change of velocity, $a = dv/dt$). Average values span a finite interval; instantaneous values are their limits as the interval shrinks — the tangent slope on a position–time graph gives instantaneous velocity, the tangent slope on a velocity–time graph…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - v = dr/dt; a = dv/dt - Average: v_av = Δr/Δt; a_av = Δv/Δt - Uniform a: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Limit Definition Universality:** Instantaneous velocity $v = dx/dt$ and acceleration $a = dv/dt$ are defined as limits ($\Delta t o 0$). They apply to *any* motion — uniform or non-uniform, constant or variable acceleration. The SUVAT equations ($v = u + at$, etc.) are special cases valid *only* for constant $a$.  ·  **Graph Duality — Slopes vs Areas:** On $x$-$t$ graph: slope of tangent = $v$. On $v$-$t$ graph: slope of tangent = $a$; area under curve = displacement. On $a$-$t$ graph: area under curve = change in velocity. Mixing up slope/area is the most common graph error.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Note 1: Carry units through calculus: if $x$ is in metres and $t$ in seconds, $v$ is m/s and $a$ is m/s² automatically.  ·  Note 2: NEB graph questions award marks for BOTH slope reasoning and area reasoning — label which you used.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Car from rest to 20 m/s in 10 s*** — a = 2 m/s², s = 100 m (NEB 2014).

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **Speed vs velocity:** speed is the scalar path-length rate; velocity is the vector displacement rate — equal only in straight-line motion without reversal.  ·  **Zero velocity vs zero acceleration:** at the top of a vertical throw v = 0 but a = g downward; in uniform velocity motion a = 0.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Task 1: Differentiate five polynomial position functions, evaluating $v$ and $a$ at specified instants.  ·  Task 2: Sketch $x$–$t$, $v$–$t$ and $a$–$t$ triplet graphs for: uniform motion, uniformly accelerated motion, and simple back-and-forth motion.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "Slope of x–t gives v; slope of v–t gives a; area under v–t gives s."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Numerical (3m): A car moving at 10 m/s accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s² for 4 s. Find the final velocity and distance travelled.** — v = u + at = 10 + 2×4 = 18 m/s; s = ut + ½at² = 10×4 + ½×2×16 = 40 + 16 = 56 m (NEB 2023).

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Most-tested: definitions (2024) and two-equation numericals (2014, 2023). Graph-reading questions use slopes and areas.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **The limit is the idea:** instantaneous values are average values over an interval shrunk to zero — the derivative before calculus names it.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Instantaneous velocity v = dr/dt (slope of x–t tangent); instantaneous acceleration a = dv/dt (slope of v–t tangent).  ·  Area under v–t graph = displacement.  ·  Uniform acceleration numericals: a = (v−u)/t; s = ut + ½at².

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: A body can move with increasing speed and decreasing acceleration — acceleration measures how fast velocity changes, not how large velocity is.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — From Average to Instantaneous A car's speedometer does not show its average speed over the whole trip; it shows the velocity **right now**. Defining velocity and acceleration at an instant — as limits of shrinking time intervals — is the conceptual heart of kinematics, and the gateway to calculus-based physics.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2024) | Quantity | Definition | Unit | Nature | |---|---|---|---| | **Position** ($\vec r$) | Location relative to an origin, with direction | m | Vector | | **Displacement** ($\Delta\vec r$) | Change of position: final − initial | m | Vector | | **Average velocity** | $\vec v_{av} = \Delta\vec r/\Delta t$ over a finite interval | m/s | Vector |…  ·  ## 3. Graphical Meaning - On a **position–time graph**, instantaneous velocity is the **slope of the tangent** at that instant (average velocity is the slope of the chord). - On a **velocity–time graph**, instantaneous acceleration is the slope of the tangent; the **area under the v–t curve** gives displacement.…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **Sign Logic for Speeding/Slowing:** Speeding up $\Leftrightarrow$ $v$ and $a$ have *same* sign. Slowing down $\Leftrightarrow$ $v$ and $a$ have *opposite* signs. This is true regardless of coordinate choice. At a turning point ($v=0$), $a eq 0$ (e.g., ball at top of flight: $v=0$, $a=g$).  ·  Note 3: When integrating acceleration, always determine integration constants from given initial conditions.  ·  Note 4: In 'is the particle speeding up?' questions, compare signs of $v$ and $a$ at that instant — not the sign of $a$ alone.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Verified PYQs: define position/velocity/acceleration (2024, 2m); uniform-acceleration numerical (2014, 3m).  ·  "The speedometer reads instantaneous speed; the odometer averages."  ·  Can a body have constant speed and non-zero acceleration?
